# Final engineering report: Security Guardrail Middleware

## What was built
A Python package, `guardrails`, and an optional FastAPI service around it. It checks text going into a model, text coming out,
retrieved content, and tool calls made by agents. Each check returns one of four actions: allow, sanitize, require_review, block.
It uses no model and no network by default. Layout: `docs/architecture.md`. How to run: `README.md`.

## Numbers (from `docs/evaluation_results.md`, generated by `python -m evaluation run`)
<!-- numbers: all_bad=172/309; benign_fp=10/128 -->
* Bad cases handled correctly: **172 of 309 (55.7%, 95% CI 50.1% to 61.1%)**.
* Normal texts wrongly changed or blocked: **10 of 128 (7.8%, 95% CI 4.3% to 13.8%)**.
* Sensitive values still present in released text: 14.

| Category | Handled correctly |
|---|---|
| prompt injection | 81 of 196 (41.3%) |
| secrets | 39 of 46 (84.8%) |
| personal data | 31 of 41 (75.6%) |
| unsafe content | 14 of 17 (82.4%) |
| system prompt leak | 7 of 9 (77.8%) |

Hand-written injection cases: 31 of 126 (24.6%). Generated variants of known patterns: 50 of 70 (71.4%). The gap shows the rules are good at what their author thought of and weak elsewhere.
Speed on the development machine (one thread): 20,000-character inputs about 47 ms typical, 73 ms slowest of the deliberately slow inputs tried.

**These numbers are optimistic.** The set is small, written by the same person as the rules, and was used to tune them (a dev and held-out split exists, but it is not an independent test). Treat them as a regression guard, not as expected real-world performance.

Test suite at the end of Phase 14 (run here, Linux, Python 3.13): 866 passed, 8 expected failures (documented limits, marked strict). No test uses a paid model or the network.

## What works well
* Controls that do not depend on guessing: size and depth limits, strict argument validation, role and tenant checks, single-use approvals, key scopes, fixed-text errors, no content in logs or metrics.
* Fail closed by default, with tests that break the detector, audit log and limiter on purpose.
* Mutation checks on the key safeguards (a deliberately broken safeguard makes a test fail), and strict xfail tests that record known gaps so they cannot be forgotten.

## Limitations (what not to claim)
* **Do not claim the system stops prompt injection.** It catches a minority of the cases tried. Design the host application so that an injected model cannot do harm: least-privilege tools, approvals, output checks.
* Do not claim complete PII or secret protection. Pattern detectors miss unknown formats and paraphrases.
* State is per process (rate limits, runs, budgets). Several workers need external shared limits.
* The audit chain detects edits in the middle, not removal of the end without a saved head.
* Docker image and CI workflow were never built or executed in the development environment.
* No independent review or penetration test was done. No load test beyond a single-machine timing table.
* Only text. No images, files, audio.

## Decisions worth knowing
Deterministic rules first; a model-based detector is optional and off by default. Production defaults refuse unsafe settings. Decisions never hold the matched text. An `allow` rule cannot waive secrets.

## Suggested next steps
1. Replace the evaluation set with cases written by someone else, and add real (consented, redacted) traffic samples.
2. Add a trained classifier as an optional second layer and measure it with the same harness.
3. Shared rate-limit and approval state (for example a database or cache) for multi-instance use.
4. Build and run the container and CI; add a key revocation endpoint.

The Definition-of-Done matrix has 12 items Met and 4 Partly. The Partly ones are monitoring (no OpenTelemetry adapter, never connected to the real dashboard), CI (never run), adversarial coverage, and regression across the earlier projects (not re-run).

See also: `docs/definition_of_done.md`, `docs/security.md`, `docs/phase13.md`.
